title: I am discussing vitals.
author: M37R_TI
selftext:
I am a gamer.  I am absolutely against the use of generative AI. I hate it to death. Despite this, I'm curious about the reason why you incorporated artificial intelligence into the game development process.

You can design mechanisms. You can write the story; (but some of you don't even do that.). You can create the conflict required for the game. You can build the system. But the art direction does not belong to you, and the game feeling/game experience/immersive elements do not belong to you either, because the art component makes up 90% of the game feeling and immersiveness. You can make stupid compliments by making excuses like "AI is very useful to me," "I'm not good at drawing," "I don't understand the art part," and "I don't have time." But you cannot claim credit for the sweat you didn't shed or the labor that didn't exist. Involving artificial intelligence in the work is laziness. It is also a betrayal of humanity. Because while artificial intelligences were being trained, everyone's data, the cultural accumulation of humanity, was stolen. The sleazy billionaires who trained artificial intelligence used, that is, stole, works of art of immeasurable spiritual value in violation of copyright laws. And you're just using something that was stolen and melted down and refined into a training data pool. Not a work of art.

replies.author: M37R_TI
replies.body:
You are conflating human learning and inspiration with systematic theft.

When someone shares open-source code or free assets online, they do so willingly under specific terms. Even then, if you want to adapt that work to your game, it demands real human labor: you either put in the hours to learn the craft, or you pay someone who did. You actually transform it with intent.

Generative AI doesn't 'learn' like a human studying game mechanics. It ingests millions of copyrighted, non-consensual works without compensating a single creator.  It launders that stolen labor, completely erases attribution, and circumvents the fundamental rule of creation: that transformation requires effort.

Taking someone's uncredited labor because you lack the skill or patience to draw isn't an 'industry shortcut'—it’s just exploitation masquerading as efficiency

comments.author: Fincut
comments.body:
You say you’re curious why people use AI, but your post answers the question before anyone can. If the answer is “laziness” and “betrayal of humanity”, there is nothing left to ask. That’s not a discussion, that’s a verdict with a question mark on top. I’ll answer anyway, for the people reading along.

“Art is 90 % of the game feeling.” That depends heavily on the genre. In a tactics or strategy game, rules, balance and the quality of decisions carry most of the experience. Art matters a lot, but 90 % is a claim, not a fact.

“Using AI is laziness.” A tool says nothing about how much work went into the result. Direction, testing, iteration and taste still take hundreds of hours. People said the same about sampling, procedural generation and engines.

“Betrayal of humanity.” That’s a moral position and you’re entitled to it. But “AI” covers very different uses. A code assistant, an image generator and a music generator are not the same thing, and lumping them together makes it impossible to talk about what is actually objectionable.

Training data: your concern is legitimate. Whether it counts as theft under copyright law is still being decided in courts, and rulings differ. Artists deserve a real answer on consent and compensation, not a shrug.

From my own experience: I’m not a programmer. Without AI I would never have built the game I’d been dreaming of for years. It took me around 300 hours of directing, testing and correcting, and I’m open about where AI was used and where it wasn’t. That seems to me a better basis for judging a project than an assumption.

If you really want to understand why people do this, I’m glad to talk. If you only want to confirm what you already think, I’ll leave it here.

comments.author: muikrad
comments.body:
The difficult part of making a good game isn't the code and isn't the graphics either. Even if AI can nail the code and to some extent, the graphics, doesn't mean it can nail a good game, or even a complete game for that matter; one that feature good story, plot, quests, levels, puzzles. And also the game has to feel satisfying, rewarding and the controls and execution must feel good. 

All these things, AI cannot help. It will lay down bases, but ultimately it is still the human that must refine everything into a good game.

And then you have to market it and sell it, which is a whole different game to play.

You are actually very insulting of game devs, AI or not, if you think a game is just about graphics and code. AI lowered the bar of entry to game development it didn't solve gaming.

Now about the other part of your post, the "stolen" part, well, that's a price we had to pay to be able to train such a wonderful tool. And it's definitely a shame for artists, but world-changing inventions like that happened several times over the course of human history. If you're holding a grudge against that, you're clearly not seeing farther than your own ego. What you see here in AI is the combination of all the talents of humanity. You can either see that as a threat, or as a marvel.

comments.author: Kojinto
comments.body:
I'll try to give you a real response and it's going to be voice to text so it's going to be rough. I use AI especially Claude Opus 5.5 because God damn, but I use AI because I've always had the mind and the want to design and build games ever since I was a kid. I'd make like little RPG games on pieces of notebook paper with dice sometimes even Domino's, but as I grew up it became harder to focus and it wasn't until the past 6 years that I learned I had ADHD the executive dysfunction, the whole Gambit. 

And I'm also one who is not ready to explore medication for it. I've seen what the side effects do to loved ones around me who also have it and I am not interested in dealing with those side effects. That said my brain absolutely loves designing as much of my projects as possible, especially this new game I'm working on that is a combination of almost everything I've wanted out of a role playing game on a scale that I've never experienced with more aspects of simulation then I think most people have ever asked for. With the kicker being everything you do, every action you take, exploring, talking to NPCs, and combat is done by writing. The better you write the better you are at the thing that you do and the game turns your writing into a visible actionable spectacle.

And sure, I could have not gone that route because having a game based on writing will make the whole thing more niche, but not enough people read and write these days and when it comes to making games, my previous project before this was a mental math roguelite so I guess that's just something I feel like I have to do in terms of making something. That when people engage with what I make that it isn't just for entertainment but might help them a little as well. 

But it's not just the fact that there are parts of the game that I am not capable of making. I mean even though yes that is the case but it's also a case about cost. I work in fast food, it's been very hard to get out, and it's near impossible to work from home and make a decent amount of money for me, and so I've been feeling trapped for years. 

But with AI I can spend maybe at max 200 a month and a little extra for advertising or even just a hundred a month and that's enough usage to allow me to focus on building it daily. And it has become my new favorite hobby and it gives me something to think about while I'm at work hating the fact that I'm there. Especially when I can think about new things to design, or ways to improve systems and then I have a reasoning intelligence that I can go home to and talk with them about and then we make the game better. 

It feels like magic and my brain loves it and as far as I can tell I'm actually good at it. Not to toot my own horn or anything but I I made an ad for the game put it on my tiktok, did a $24 promotion over one day and my site went from 27 users to over 160 in less than a week. Not crazy numbers, but for mainly a writing game I was I was kind of blown away. I didn't really expect that so I think that's about as real of an answer as I can give you. 

Most people who are like me use AI as a way to build the things that they couldn't before and to elevate their way of life in ways that couldn't have been done before without the huge reduction of cost that comes from the labor of making such a thing. You can still make the case that like what me and others are doing are morally wrong or ethically wrong 
, sure. 

But I think the bigger morally ethically wrong thing is that we live in a society where the only way I can potentially get ahead and not feel forced into doing a different flavor of thing I hate, is by using the morally ethically wrong thing. Which is not even arguably the bigger of two evils If we compare AI to our modern capitalistic societies at large. There's no way to beat it other than to go through, And to vote for the right people, and that has not been a success as of late either. 

So I pick and choose my battles and resign to using a technology made by billionaires I hate, so that I can find ways to enjoy living life just a little more.

comments.author: Post-reality
comments.body: There's a game I dreamed about developing since the early 2000's. My younger brother knew coding and turned to become a software engineer - I used to beg him to help me develop a prototype but he failed to deliver. I even planned to hire a game studio to develop the game for me, and was even in contact with 1 studio. That game is quite complicated, and could have costed millions to develop. Yes, I even saved 7 figures worth of dollars so I can eventually hire a studio to develop this game for me. Thanks to AI, I manage to develop it myself. You make it sound so easy hahaha - no! Everything is so precise, you can't just prompt a fast action MMORPG with heavily stylized (high-quality) artstyle - Impossible. And no, using just Claude doesn't crack it - you need to use multiple models for assets (sprites, layers, sounds, animation, etc). I have been working on my game for almost 18 hours per day, 7 days per week, and I barely scratched the surface (it would take me 1-2 years to fully develop it at the current rate). So if it would take 1-2 years, working 18 hours per day, now imagine that without AI..... Yeah, it would take multiple lifetimes, if it's even possible (IMO at the current scope the game would have been impossible to develop manually due to the complexity of the multiple layers - the player's character can wear a lot pieces of clothing, and the characters themselves have hundreds of body positions). Also, I feel that AI leads to the way I wished to develop the game myself, because by the end of the day, I tell him precisely everything without adding unnecessary stuff, and if it does, then I just asjust/polish/change. That's no different to hiring someone or a studio and instructung them with ODD/game plan. I also feel like the AI is smarter and faster than traditional developers.

comments.author: Substantial-Ad-1546
comments.body:
So.. you come into a community centered on AI-assisted game development, claim that you’re curious, and then immediately insult the people here and invent their process for them?

That's not curiosity at all. You’ve already decided that anyone using AI is lazy, unskilled, stealing work, falsely claiming credit, and “betraying humanity.” You leave no room for nuance around different workflows, ethical lines, levels of effort, or creative control.

There is a meaningful difference between entering one prompt and uploading whatever comes back, and spending months directing agents, rejecting unsatisfactory results, debugging, testing, revising, and shaping everything until it meets a specific creative standard. Serious AI-assisted development is not “prompt in, game out,” no matter how convenient that framing is for you. It is a different workflow with its own labor, technical demands, and judgment.

In my case, AI makes it possible for one person to accomplish work that would ordinarily require a small team. I’m still acting as creative director, systems and mechanics designer, scenario planner, level designer, tester, and more. My art direction lives in the vision, the decisions, the revisions, what gets rejected, what survives, and responsibility for the finished work.

Not all of us use generative art assets, either. It is entirely possible to significantly expedite game development without them, and some of us do. The ethical lines and methods vary from person to person, and a serious discussion requires more than blanket accusations. At the same time, developers who work with AI are not obligated to endlessly defend their work or give attention to people who don't approach it in good faith.

You’re entitled to oppose the technology. but if you genuinely want to understand why people use it, ask about their process instead of hurling insults and making assumptions. If you’re unwilling to understand, then there is no good-faith discussion to be had.
